contentBlocks.heading: The overall scorecard
contentBlocks.body:
ACOs have produced meaningful but modest net savings. CMS data through 2023 shows MSSP ACOs generate gross savings of $2–3 billion annually, but after sharing those savings with ACOs, the net savings to Medicare are smaller — and varied by study design.

Quality performance has generally been positive: MSSP ACOs outperform FFS on preventive care measures, follow-up after hospitalization, and patient experience. High-performing ACOs consistently show improvements in diabetes management, hypertension control, and avoidable hospitalizations.

contentBlocks.heading: The benchmark problem
contentBlocks.body: A persistent criticism: MSSP benchmarks are based on each ACO's own historical spending. ACOs that were already efficient had low benchmarks — they had to become even more efficient to generate savings. Early ACO savings may have been driven partly by organizations that had been overspending entering the program and cutting waste, not structural transformation. CMS has moved to regional benchmarks to address this.

items.title: Robust primary care
items.body: High-touch primary care with care managers embedded in practices, proactive outreach to high-risk patients, and after-hours access.

items.title: Behavioral health integration
items.body: Integrated behavioral health in primary care settings — addressing depression, substance use, and mental illness that drive high utilization.

items.title: Post-acute care management
items.body: Tight relationships with skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies, and hospitalists to reduce readmissions and optimize post-hospital care.

items.title: Data analytics
items.body: Real-time claims data to identify rising-risk patients before hospitalization. ACOs without analytics struggle to target interventions.

questions.question: Why did CMS move from historical to regional benchmarks for MSSP ACOs?
questions.explanation: Historical benchmarks penalized already-efficient ACOs (they had less room to cut) and rewarded previously high-spending organizations that had easy waste to eliminate. Regional benchmarks compare ACOs to peers in their market.

contentBlocks.body: The MSSP ACO model was designed for traditional Medicare. But states and commercial payers have developed their own ACO-like models for Medicaid and commercial populations. lessons.title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 3: The Economics Pillar — Following the Money in Value-Based Care
lessons.summary: Module 3 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the financial mechanics of value-based care from first principles. Learners will leave this module able to evaluate a VBC contract term sheet, identify the key actuarial concepts their finance teams are using, and understand the economic case for primary care investment as the highest-return infrastructure spend in healthcare.

contentBlocks.body:
The Medicare Shared Savings Program is the most widely adopted VBC model in the United States, and shared savings is the financial mechanism at its core. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. contentBlocks.heading: Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything
contentBlocks.body:
One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk — where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it — or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (MSSP ENHANCED Track, Direct Contracting, ACO REACH) offer higher shared savings percentages — sometimes up to 80% of savings — but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1–3% of benchmark spending.

contentBlocks.body:
Bundled payment models take a different economic approach to aligning incentives than shared savings. Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode — typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable. — Leemore Dafny, Harvard Business School, Health Affairs, 2025.

Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month — the “PMPM” rate — and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. contentBlocks.heading: The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy
contentBlocks.body:
The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period — the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure — care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program — that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population’s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.

contentBlocks.body: For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. contentBlocks.heading: Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure
contentBlocks.body:
One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.

The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

The ROI data in the table above carries an important caveat: these are population-level averages from mature ACOs that have already built the data infrastructure to identify high-risk patients, target interventions appropriately, and measure outcomes accurately. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.

Care coordinators assigned to high-risk patients generate the highest absolute savings per dollar invested, but their effectiveness depends entirely on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.

Post-discharge follow-up programs have the highest ROI ratio of any single intervention (4.6x) because the cost of a 72-hour phone call is minimal relative to the cost of a readmission, and the evidence that timely follow-up reduces readmissions is among the strongest in care management research.

Community health worker integration produces the largest absolute savings per patient ($1,260 net benefit annually) and is the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change.

Advanced primary care transformation has the highest total annual investment per patient ($580) but also the highest total annual savings ($2,140), making it the most comprehensive single intervention for organizations ready to redesign their primary care delivery model rather than simply add discrete programs to an unchanged clinical workflow.

contentBlocks.body: The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top. — Mark McClellan, Duke-Margolis Center for Health Policy, JAMA, 2025.

contentBlocks.heading: Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision
contentBlocks.body:
The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.

The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is clear in the mature ACO data: organizations in their fifth year of MSSP participation generate average shared savings payments of $312 per beneficiary at an investment cost of $87 per beneficiary, a 3.6-to-1 return that compounds as the care management infrastructure matures and the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients improves. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.

Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.

Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.

Review the ROI data from the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.

Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track or ACO REACH participation is warranted.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.

One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.

The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

children.text: The ROI data in the table above carries an important caveat: these are population-level averages from mature ACOs that have already built the data infrastructure to identify high-risk patients, target interventions appropriately, and measure outcomes accurately. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.

Care coordinators assigned to high-risk patients generate the highest absolute savings per dollar invested, but their effectiveness depends entirely on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.

Post-discharge follow-up programs have the highest ROI ratio of any single intervention (4.6x) because the cost of a 72-hour phone call is minimal relative to the cost of a readmission, and the evidence that timely follow-up reduces readmissions is among the strongest in care management research.

Community health worker integration produces the largest absolute savings per patient ($1,260 net benefit annually) and is the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change.

Advanced primary care transformation has the highest total annual investment per patient ($580) but also the highest total annual savings ($2,140), making it the most comprehensive single intervention for organizations ready to redesign their primary care delivery model rather than simply add discrete programs to an unchanged clinical workflow.

The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top. — Mark McClellan, Duke-Margolis Center for Health Policy, JAMA, 2025.
Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision

The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.

The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is clear in the mature ACO data: organizations in their fifth year of MSSP participation generate average shared savings payments of $312 per beneficiary at an investment cost of $87 per beneficiary, a 3.6-to-1 return that compounds as the care management infrastructure matures and the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients improves. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.

Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.

Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.

Review the ROI data from the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.

Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track or ACO REACH participation is warranted.

Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.

tracks.title: Bundled Payments
tracks.description: How episode-based bundled payments work, the BPCI Advanced program, which conditions are best suited to bundling, and the evidence on bundle outcomes.

lessons.title: Episode-Based Bundled Payments: How They Work
lessons.summary: The mechanics of bundled payments — episode definition, anchor event, spending window, reconciliation — and which clinical conditions have seen the strongest results.

objectives.text: Explain what a bundled payment episode is and how it is defined
Describe the BPCI Advanced program and which conditions it covers
Explain why post-acute care is the primary savings lever in most bundles

contentBlocks.heading: Paying for the whole episode, not each piece
contentBlocks.body:
A bundled payment sets a single price for all care related to a defined episode — for example, a hip replacement plus 90 days of follow-up care. If the hospital and its partners spend less than the bundle price while meeting quality thresholds, they keep the difference. If they overspend, they owe the difference back.

Bundled payments differ from ACOs in scope: ACOs take accountability for all care for a population over a year. Bundles take accountability for one specific episode — a surgery, a hospitalization for heart failure, a chemotherapy course — plus a defined post-acute window.

items.title: Anchor event
items.body: The triggering hospitalization or procedure (e.g., total knee arthroplasty) that begins the episode.

items.title: Episode window
items.body: The time period included in the bundle — typically 30, 60, or 90 days post-anchor. All related care during this window falls within the bundle.

items.title: Target price
items.body: The pre-determined spending target for the episode, based on historical spending adjusted for clinical and geographic factors.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.body: At the end of the performance period, CMS compares actual spending to target. The participant repays overspending or receives a share of savings.

contentBlocks.heading: Post-acute care: where the money is
contentBlocks.body: In most bundled payment conditions, post-acute care (skilled nursing facilities, home health, inpatient rehab) accounts for 40–60% of episode costs. The largest savings opportunity is not in the surgery itself but in reducing unnecessarily long SNF stays, shifting patients to lower-cost settings, and preventing readmissions. High-performing bundle participants carefully manage where patients go after discharge.

contentBlocks.heading: BPCI Advanced: the current Medicare bundle program
contentBlocks.body:
Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced) is CMS's current voluntary bundled payment model. Participants — hospitals or physician group practices — take two-sided risk on 32 clinical episode types, including major joint replacement, hip fracture, COPD, and acute myocardial infarction.

Successful participants have typically invested in: dedicated care coordinators who follow patients from hospital to post-acute, preferred SNF networks with data-sharing agreements, and real-time tracking of episode spending.

questions.explanation: Post-acute care (skilled nursing facilities, home health, inpatient rehab) typically accounts for 40–60% of episode costs and represents the largest savings lever.

lessons.title: Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows
lessons.summary: The evidence on bundled payment performance across conditions — where bundles have saved money, improved quality, and reduced disparities, and where they have failed.

objectives.text: Summarize the evidence on BPCI savings across major clinical episode types
Explain the equity concerns with bundled payment programs

contentBlocks.heading: The strongest evidence: major joint replacement
contentBlocks.body:
The most robust evidence for bundled payment savings comes from major joint replacement (hip and knee arthroplasty). Studies of BPCI and its predecessor programs show consistent savings of 5–10% on total episode costs, primarily through reduced post-acute spending and lower readmission rates.

Successful joint replacement bundle participants share common features: they established preferred post-acute networks with aligned SNFs, implemented discharge criteria that shifted appropriate patients to home health instead of SNF, and hired care navigators who tracked patients through the 90-day window.

contentBlocks.heading: Equity concern: who avoids complex patients?
contentBlocks.body: A persistent equity critique of bundled payments: providers facing episode cost risk have financial incentives to avoid complex, high-cost patients — those with more comorbidities, lower income, or who live in areas with fewer post-acute options. Studies have found evidence of patient selection in cardiac and orthopedic bundles. CMS has tried to address this through risk adjustment, but critics argue it is insufficient.

lessons.title: The Oncology Care Model: VBC in Cancer Care
lessons.summary: CMS's Oncology Care Model (OCM) and its successor Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM) — how episode-based payment has been applied to cancer chemotherapy and the evidence on performance.

objectives.text: Describe the Oncology Care Model's payment structure
Explain the equity concerns specific to VBC in oncology
Summarize what the OCM evidence showed about savings and quality

contentBlocks.heading: Applying episode payment to cancer
contentBlocks.body:
Cancer care is among the most expensive areas of US healthcare — and among the most difficult to apply episode-based payment models to. Treatment courses vary enormously, clinical pathways are rapidly evolving, and drug costs have been exploding.

The Oncology Care Model (OCM, 2016–2022) covered 6-month episodes anchored by chemotherapy initiation. Practices received a $160/month per-beneficiary-per-month payment for care management, plus shared savings or losses against a benchmark. 187 practices participated at peak.

contentBlocks.heading: OCM results: minimal savings, quality improvement
contentBlocks.body: The final OCM evaluation found minimal net savings to Medicare — about 0.2% of episode costs in the best-performing cohort. However, quality improvements were meaningful: participating practices showed higher hospice use, fewer ED visits, and better symptom documentation. The successor Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM, 2023–) focuses on a smaller set of high-cost cancers with a modified payment approach.

items.title: Patient selection risk
items.body: Practices may avoid enrolling complex patients with more comorbidities or limited social support who are more likely to generate losses.

items.title: Geography
items.body: Rural practices lack post-acute partners and palliative care resources that urban practices can leverage to control episode costs.

items.title: Racial disparities
items.body: Black cancer patients have historically received less aggressive treatment. VBP models that reward cost reduction must ensure they don't reinforce undertreatment.

items.title: Drug costs
items.body: Cancer drug prices have risen 10–15% annually. Episode benchmarks can be overwhelmed by new drug approvals mid-performance period.

questions.explanation: The OCM showed minimal net savings to Medicare (about 0.2% of episode costs) but meaningful quality improvements — higher hospice use, fewer ED visits.

tracks.description: How healthcare quality is measured, the measure stewards, HEDIS, eCQMs, the problems with current measurement, and the move toward patient-reported outcomes.

lessons.title: HEDIS, eCQMs & the Quality Measurement Ecosystem
lessons.summary: The landscape of quality measures — who creates them, how they are reported, what HEDIS and eCQMs are, and the ongoing debate about measure burden and meaningful measurement.

objectives.text: Distinguish between HEDIS measures and eCQMs and how each is collected
Identify the major measure stewards and their roles

contentBlocks.heading: The measurement ecosystem
contentBlocks.body: Healthcare quality measurement involves multiple organizations creating, endorsing, and reporting measures — often with different methodologies, data sources, and populations. The result is a measurement ecosystem that is rich in data but fragmented in practice.

items.title: NCQA
items.body: National Committee for Quality Assurance. Creates HEDIS measures — the most widely used quality measures in the US, reported by health plans for their populations.

items.title: CMS
items.body: Operates the eCQM (electronic clinical quality measure) program, the Hospital Compare reporting system, and ties measures to payment in VBC programs.

items.title: NQF
items.body: National Quality Forum. Endorses measures through a consensus process — NQF endorsement is required for many federal quality programs.

items.title: Specialty societies
items.body: ACC, ACS, AHA and others create specialty-specific registry measures that complement HEDIS and eCQMs for cardiology, oncology, etc.

contentBlocks.heading: Measure burden: the 15-minute visit problem
contentBlocks.body: Physicians now spend an estimated 15+ hours per week on documentation and reporting requirements. Studies show that every patient visit generates 2+ hours of EHR time. CMS has acknowledged the problem and has been actively sunsetting low-value measures, aligning measure sets across programs, and investing in digital quality measure infrastructure to reduce manual reporting burden.

lessons.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes: Measuring What Patients Care About
lessons.summary: The shift from clinician-measured to patient-reported outcomes (PROs), the PROMIS framework, CMS's use of PROs in VBC programs, and the implementation challenges.

objectives.text: Explain what patient-reported outcomes are and why they matter for quality measurement
Describe the PROMIS measurement framework and its advantages
Identify how CMS is incorporating PROs into value-based care programs

contentBlocks.heading: What the patient experiences matters most
contentBlocks.body:
Most quality measures capture process (did we do the recommended thing?) or intermediate outcome (did the patient's A1c improve?). Rarely do they ask: how does the patient feel? Can they do what they want to do? Is their pain tolerable? These patient-reported outcomes (PROs) capture the dimensions of health that patients care about most — and that don't appear in clinical records.

PROs are collected via validated questionnaires asking patients directly about their symptoms, function, and quality of life. They are distinct from satisfaction surveys (CAHPS) — PROs measure health states, not opinions about care.

items.title: PROMIS
items.body: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System. NIH-funded standardized measures across physical function, fatigue, pain, depression, anxiety, social functioning. Calibrated by item response theory — adaptive short-form versions available.

items.title: KOOS/HOOS
items.body: Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score / Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score. Condition-specific PROs used in orthopedic bundles and joint replacement episodes.

items.title: ICHOM sets
items.body: International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement. Condition-specific standard outcome sets developed with patient input — used globally to enable comparison across health systems.

contentBlocks.heading: CMS's move toward PROs
contentBlocks.body: CMS has begun incorporating PROs into several programs: joint replacement bundles require functional outcome reporting, MIPS has PRO-based quality measures, and the ACO PC Flex model incorporates patient experience measures. The challenge: collecting PROs at scale requires patient portal infrastructure, engagement, and support for patients with limited digital access.

questions.question: What distinguishes patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from patient satisfaction surveys like CAHPS?
questions.explanation: PROs measure health states — symptoms, function, quality of life as experienced by the patient. CAHPS measures patient experience and satisfaction with care delivery, not health status.

tracks.title: Risk Adjustment
tracks.description: Why risk adjustment is essential to fair value-based payment, how HCC-based risk scoring works, and the gaming and equity problems with current models.

lessons.title: Risk Adjustment & HCC Scores: Leveling the Playing Field
lessons.summary: Why risk adjustment is necessary for fair VBC payment, how Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCCs) work, how risk scores affect revenue, and the upcoding controversy.

objectives.text: Explain why risk adjustment is necessary for fair comparison in VBC
Describe how HCC-based risk scores are calculated
Explain the upcoding problem and its consequences for the program

contentBlocks.heading: The selection problem
contentBlocks.body:
Without risk adjustment, value-based payment rewards providers who serve healthy patients and penalizes those who serve the sickest. A primary care practice that attracts many elderly patients with multiple chronic conditions will spend more on their care — not because they're inefficient, but because their patients need more care.

Risk adjustment solves this by adjusting payment targets (and quality measure comparisons) based on predicted spending for each patient's health status. A provider with sicker patients gets a higher benchmark; one with healthier patients gets a lower one.

contentBlocks.heading: HCC risk scores: how they're built
contentBlocks.body:
CMS uses a Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) model to calculate each Medicare beneficiary's risk score (Risk Adjustment Factor, or RAF). The model works like this:

1. Claims are submitted by providers with ICD-10 diagnosis codes
2. Diagnoses map to one of 86 HCC categories (e.g., HCC 19 = diabetes without complications, HCC 18 = diabetes with chronic complications)
3. Each HCC has a coefficient representing its contribution to predicted spending
4. The sum of all a patient's HCC coefficients plus demographic factors = their RAF score
5. RAF 1.0 = average cost; RAF 2.0 = twice average cost

Organizations in risk-based contracts are paid based on their population's average RAF — higher RAF populations receive higher per-member-per-month payments.

contentBlocks.heading: The upcoding problem
contentBlocks.body: Because RAF scores translate directly to revenue, there are strong financial incentives to ensure all diagnoses are captured — and, in some cases, to document conditions that may be questionable. OIG and DOJ investigations have found that Medicare Advantage plans (which also use HCC-based risk adjustment) have overstated member acuity by billions of dollars annually through systematic upcoding. CMS has responded with stricter audits and risk score adjustments.

lessons.title: Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?
lessons.summary: The contested question of whether to include social risk factors in clinical quality risk adjustment — arguments on both sides and the NASEM recommendations.

objectives.text: Explain the argument for including social risk factors in quality measure risk adjustment
Explain the argument against adjusting for social risk
Summarize the NASEM recommendations on social risk adjustment

contentBlocks.heading: The core tension
contentBlocks.body:
Risk adjustment corrects for clinical complexity so that providers caring for sicker patients aren't unfairly penalized on quality or cost measures. The question: should social risk factors — poverty, housing instability, limited English proficiency — be adjusted for in the same way?

Providers argue yes: safety-net hospitals and practices caring for high-poverty populations face structural barriers to quality outcomes that have nothing to do with the quality of their care. Adjusting for social risk levels the playing field.

Equity advocates argue no: adjusting for poverty sets lower quality expectations for poor patients — essentially accepting worse care for the disadvantaged. The goal should be to close gaps, not to hide them.

contentBlocks.heading: Arguments for and against social risk adjustment

rows.label: Fairness
rows.left: Providers caring for high-social-risk patients face barriers beyond their control
rows.right: Adjustment accepts lower quality expectations for poor patients

rows.label: Access
rows.left: Without adjustment, providers may avoid high-risk populations to protect scores
rows.right: Incentives to improve social determinants may be reduced if gaps are adjusted away

rows.label: Accountability
rows.left: Penalizing safety-net providers unfairly may close them, harming access further
rows.right: Accountability requires measuring actual outcomes without excusing poor performance

contentBlocks.heading: NASEM's 2017 recommendation: stratify, don't adjust
contentBlocks.body: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) recommended stratifying quality measure results by social risk — reporting performance separately for high and low social risk patients — rather than adjusting measures to reduce apparent gaps. This preserves accountability for all providers while revealing where disparities exist. CMS has moved toward this approach.

questions.question: What did NASEM recommend for handling social risk in quality measurement?
questions.explanation: NASEM recommended stratifying quality measure results by social risk — reporting separately for high and low social risk patients — rather than adjusting measures to hide gaps.

options.text: Adjust all quality measures for social risk factors in addition to clinical risk
Stratify results by social risk to reveal disparities while preserving accountability
Exclude safety-net providers from quality measurement programs entirely

tracks.title: Star Ratings & Consumer Transparency
tracks.description: How CMS Star Ratings work for Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, what's in the 5-star formula, and how Star Ratings drive plan behavior and consumer choice.

lessons.title: Medicare Advantage Star Ratings: Formula, Stakes & Strategy
lessons.summary: How CMS calculates 1-5 star ratings for Medicare Advantage plans, what the financial stakes are, and how plans manage their star strategy.

objectives.text: Explain the 5-star rating formula and its major domains
Describe the financial consequences of star rating levels for MA plans
Identify the measures with the highest weight and strategic importance

contentBlocks.heading: Stars as a market signal and a financial lever
contentBlocks.body:
CMS rates every Medicare Advantage and Part D plan on a 1–5 star scale, published annually on Medicare.gov. Stars serve two purposes: consumer transparency (beneficiaries can compare plans) and financial incentives (CMS pays quality bonuses to plans rated 4 stars or above).

The stakes are enormous. A plan earning 4+ stars receives a 5% bonus on its base payment rate — worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually for large plans. Plans below 3 stars for three consecutive years can be terminated from Medicare Advantage.

items.title: Staying healthy
items.body: Preventive screenings and vaccines — mammograms, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccines, annual wellness visits.

items.title: Managing chronic conditions
items.body: HEDIS measures for diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, COPD, and mental health medication adherence.

items.title: Plan responsiveness
items.body: CAHPS member experience measures — getting needed care, getting care quickly, rating of health care, customer service.

items.title: Member complaints & appeals
items.body: Complaint rates, appeals upheld, call center performance metrics.

items.title: Health plan administration
items.body: Compliance with CMS rules, pricing accuracy, and formulary compliance for Part D.

contentBlocks.heading: Highest-weight measures: where plans focus
contentBlocks.body: CMS assigns different weights to different measures — some count 3x, 4x, or 5x in the final calculation. The highest-weight measures include medication adherence for chronic conditions, care for older adults, and care transitions. Plans invest most heavily in improving these measures because the return on a star improvement is highest.

contentBlocks.label: Stars program director: what moves the needle
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a Medicare Advantage quality director about which star measures are hardest to move, what interventions have worked, and how the star program has changed plan behavior. Recommended: 8–10 minutes.

questions.question: What is the financial benefit for a Medicare Advantage plan that earns 4 or more stars?
questions.explanation: Plans rated 4+ stars receive a 5% quality bonus on their base payment rate from CMS — a significant financial incentive that drives plan investment in quality improvement.

They receive a 5% quality bonus on their base payment rate
They can charge higher premiums to beneficiaries
They receive preferred status in CMS marketing materials

lessons.title: Star Ratings & Equity: The Low-Income Subsidy Problem
lessons.summary: Why Medicare Advantage plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual eligible members consistently score lower on Star Ratings — and what CMS is doing about it.

objectives.text: Explain why plans serving LIS/dual eligible populations score lower on Star Ratings
Describe the criticism that Stars penalizes safety-net MA plans
Explain how the Health Equity Index attempts to address this

contentBlocks.heading: Stars and the equity penalty
contentBlocks.body:
Research consistently shows that Medicare Advantage plans serving higher proportions of Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries and dual eligibles score lower on Star Ratings — even after controlling for plan characteristics. This creates a troubling dynamic: plans that choose to serve the most vulnerable populations are financially penalized through lower star ratings and loss of the 5% quality bonus.

Analyses by MedPAC, CMS, and academic researchers find that 20–30% of the variance in star ratings is explained by the socioeconomic composition of a plan's enrollment — not by actual quality of care delivered.

contentBlocks.heading: The Health Equity Index: CMS's response
contentBlocks.body: Starting with 2027 Star Ratings, CMS is implementing the Health Equity Index (HEI) — a reward measure that gives plans additional credit for achieving better quality outcomes for their LIS/dual eligible and/or disability members. Plans with smaller quality gaps between vulnerable and non-vulnerable members earn HEI credit. This inverts the old incentive: rather than penalizing plans for serving difficult populations, HEI rewards plans that actually close gaps within those populations.

questions.question: What is the equity concern with the current Medicare Advantage Star Ratings system?
questions.explanation: Plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual eligible members consistently score lower on Stars, losing the quality bonus — which may discourage plans from serving these populations.

tracks.title: The Future of Value-Based Care
tracks.description: Where value-based care is heading: primary care first models, total cost of care at scale, VBC in Medicaid, and the unresolved tensions in the field.

lessons.title: Where VBC Is Heading: Primary Care, Equity & Scale
lessons.summary: The push toward primary care-centric total cost of care models, the challenge of embedding equity into VBC design, and honest assessment of what VBC has and hasn't solved.

objectives.text: Describe the AHEAD model and its significance for multi-payer VBC
Explain how VBC models can be designed to advance or inadvertently undermine equity
Articulate the honest limitations of VBC after 15 years of experimentation

contentBlocks.heading: The primary care investment deficit
contentBlocks.body: Despite 15 years of VBC, the US still underinvests in primary care relative to specialty care. Primary care receives approximately 5–7% of total health spending despite managing the majority of patient contacts. VBC models that pay for total cost of care have shown the most promise when they substantially increase primary care investment — higher per-member payments for care management, behavioral health integration, and extended access.

items.title: AHEAD Model
items.body: CMS's State All Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development (AHEAD) model. Vermont is a participant. Aligns Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers around shared total cost of care targets at the state level.

items.title: Equity in VBC
items.body: New CMS requirements for ACOs and MA plans to stratify quality data by race, ethnicity, and social risk — and to develop equity plans to close gaps.

items.title: Advanced Primary Care
items.body: CMS Primary Care First (PCF) and similar models that dramatically increase primary care revenue in exchange for total cost of care accountability.

items.title: Behavioral health integration
items.body: Collaborative Care Model payment for integrated behavioral health in primary care — finally reimbursed under CPT 99492-99494 codes.

contentBlocks.heading: What VBC has not solved
contentBlocks.body: After 15+ years of experimentation: VBC has not bent the cost curve at the population level. National health spending continues to grow faster than GDP. VBC has produced real but modest savings in specific programs. The field has learned that payment reform alone — without workforce transformation, social determinants investment, and technology alignment — is insufficient. The next chapter of VBC will need to address these structural gaps.

questions.question: What makes the AHEAD model distinct from standard ACO programs?
questions.explanation: AHEAD is a state-level multi-payer model that aligns Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers around shared total cost of care targets — unlike typical ACO programs that operate within a single payer.

lessons.title: Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland & Beyond
lessons.summary: How global hospital budgets set annual spending targets that decouple hospital revenue from volume — the Maryland Model, Vermont, and the evidence on cost and quality.

objectives.text: Explain what a global budget is and how it differs from capitation or fee-for-service
Describe Maryland's all-payer hospital global budget model and its results
Explain how global budgets change hospital incentives around volume and prevention

contentBlocks.heading: The hospital volume problem
contentBlocks.body:
In fee-for-service, hospitals earn revenue when patients are admitted. They lose revenue when patients avoid hospitalization — through better primary care, prevention, or care management. Global budgets fundamentally change this: a hospital receives a fixed annual budget regardless of how many patients it admits. If it can keep patients healthy and out of the hospital, it keeps the budget. If volume rises above target, it must absorb the additional cost.

This is the most complete form of hospital payment reform — aligning hospital financial incentives with population health for the first time.

contentBlocks.heading: Maryland: the only all-payer global budget state
contentBlocks.body:
Maryland has had a unique hospital payment system since 1977. The Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) sets hospital rates for all payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial — under a federal waiver. In 2014, Maryland entered the Total Cost of Care Model, adding a population-level global budget for Medicare spending across all care settings.

Results after 5 years: Maryland hospitals generated $1.2B in Medicare savings, achieved lower per-capita cost growth than national trends, and showed quality improvements — particularly in preventable hospitalizations and readmissions. Vermont's AHEAD model, which Vermont entered in 2024, is modeled partly on Maryland's approach.

lessons.title: From Volume to Value at the Bedside: How Value-Based Care Transforms Clinical Practice
lessons.summary: Value-based care is not just a billing change — it reshapes what happens in every exam room, every hospital ward, and every care team huddle. This module explores how the shift from fee-for-service to value changes clinical workflows, team structures, quality measurement, population health management, and care coordination. If you practice, manage, or support clinical care in any setting, this module explains why the ground is shifting beneath your feet — and what to do about it.

objectives.text: Explain how fee-for-service versus value-based payment creates different clinical incentives and workflows
Identify the four major domains of quality measurement used in VBC contracts
Define population health management and describe how it works in a primary care setting
Explain what care coordination involves and why it reduces both cost and harm
Describe evidence-based interventions that reduce preventable hospitalizations and readmissions
Identify Vermont-specific clinical programs that operationalize value-based care

children.text: Picture a primary care physician seeing 24 patients in a day. Under fee-for-service, she is rewarded for each visit, each test ordered, each referral made. Under value-based care, she is rewarded for something harder to measure but far more important: whether her patients are actually healthier. That shift in incentives changes everything that happens in the exam room.

This module is about the clinical side of the VBC transformation. It is not abstract. The shift shows up in care team huddles, in how discharge plans are written, in how nurses manage phone calls with patients just released from the hospital, and in how a physician spends the last five minutes of every appointment. Understanding these changes is essential for anyone who works in, manages, or influences clinical care.

sanityBody.title: Why Clinical Practice Must Change

stats.label: Preventable Hospital Admissions
stats.context: Roughly 1 in 4 hospital admissions in the US is considered preventable — avoidable with better outpatient management. Source: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

stats.label: 30-Day Readmission Rate
stats.context: 1 in 5 Medicare patients is readmitted within 30 days of discharge — often due to poor care transitions, not clinical failure. Source: CMS, 2023.

stats.label: Annual Chronic Disease Spend
stats.context: The US spends over $528 billion annually on the top 10 chronic diseases — almost all of which are manageable or preventable in primary care. Source: Milken Institute.

children.text: How Payment Models Shape Clinical Decisions

Clinicians do not consciously think 'I am going to order this test because I will get paid for it.' But payment systems create incentive structures that shape behavior in powerful ways. Under fee-for-service, a busy practice survives by filling the schedule. Under value-based care, a practice is rewarded for keeping patients healthy enough that they do not need to come back as often.

sanityBody.concept: How payment models shape clinical behavior
sanityBody.analogy: Think about two gyms. The first gym charges you every time you visit — the more you visit, the more they earn. They are motivated to have you come back constantly. The second gym charges a flat monthly fee — they earn the same whether you come twice a week or never. But if you quit because you are not getting healthier, they lose your membership. That gym is motivated to actually get you fit.
sanityBody.bridge: Fee-for-service is the first gym — providers earn more when you come back. Value-based care is the second gym — providers earn more when you stay healthy and do not need to come back. The incentives point in opposite directions, and that shapes clinical practice in profound ways.

sanityBody.title: Clinical Practice: Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care

rows.left: Volume of visits and procedures billed
rows.right: Patient outcomes and quality performance scores

rows.left: Reactive — treat flare-ups as they occur
rows.right: Proactive — prevent flare-ups with regular monitoring

children.text: These differences are not just philosophical. They have real operational consequences. A practice moving to value-based contracts must restructure its workflows, hire different staff — care coordinators, community health workers, data analysts — and invest in systems that identify which patients are at risk before they land in the emergency room.
Quality Measures: How Clinical Performance Is Evaluated

In value-based care, clinicians and practices are evaluated on a structured set of quality measures — standardized metrics that assess whether patients are receiving evidence-based care and achieving good outcomes. These come from several sources: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the National Committee for Quality Assurance, and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

Quality Measure: A standardized, evidence-based metric used to assess whether patients receive recommended care. Examples: the percentage of diabetic patients with HbA1c under 8.0%, the percentage of patients with hypertension whose blood pressure is controlled, or the percentage of eligible patients who received a colorectal cancer screening.

There are hundreds of quality measures in use across the US healthcare system. For primary care practices in most VBC contracts, a core set of 10 to 20 measures typically drives the bulk of performance-based bonuses or penalties. The most important fall into four categories.

sanityBody.title: The Four Domains of Clinical Quality in Value-Based Care

steps.title: Preventive Care
steps.description: Did patients receive recommended screenings and immunizations? Examples: mammography rates, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccine administration, pediatric well-child visits. These measures track whether clinicians are proactively catching problems early.

steps.title: Chronic Disease Management
steps.description: Are patients with ongoing conditions managed to target levels? Examples: HbA1c control for diabetics, blood pressure control for hypertension patients, statin therapy for cardiovascular patients. These measures track whether care prevents deterioration.

steps.title: Patient Experience
steps.description: Do patients feel heard, respected, and well-informed? Measured via standardized CAHPS surveys. Tracks communication quality, care coordination experience, and overall satisfaction. Poor scores often signal care gaps.

steps.title: Avoidable Utilization
steps.description: Are patients using the ER and hospital for things that could be handled in outpatient settings? Examples: ED visit rate for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions, 30-day readmission rate, potentially preventable admissions. High rates signal gaps in primary care access or management.

sanityBody.misconception: Quality measures are just bureaucratic checkboxes that distract from real clinical care.
sanityBody.reality: Well-designed quality measures are derived from clinical evidence. A practice that achieves high HbA1c control rates has fewer diabetic patients with amputations, kidney failure, and blindness. The measures exist because doing them consistently saves lives. The legitimate concern is ensuring that measures focus on the right things — and that they do not create perverse incentives of their own.

children.text: The most sophisticated VBC programs now move beyond process measures — did we do the right thing? — toward outcome measures: did the patient get better? Vermont's All-Payer Model tracks outcomes like population-level diabetes prevalence trends and preventable hospitalization rates, not just whether a doctor ordered a hemoglobin A1c test.
Population Health Management: Responsibility Beyond the Appointment

One of the most fundamental shifts in value-based care is moving from patient-by-patient thinking to population-level thinking. Under fee-for-service, a physician's responsibility begins when a patient walks through the door and ends when they leave. Under VBC, a care team is responsible for the health of an entire attributed patient panel — including the people who are not coming in.

sanityBody.analogy: A school principal does not just react to students who show up in her office with problems. She monitors attendance rates, tracks which students are falling behind, identifies patterns of absenteeism, and proactively reaches out to struggling families before a student drops out. She manages the entire school population — not just the ones who knock on her door.
sanityBody.bridge: Population health management works the same way. A VBC practice does not just treat patients who schedule appointments. It monitors the health status of its entire panel — flagging patients overdue for a screening, whose blood pressure has not been checked in 18 months, or whose recent ER visits suggest they are struggling to manage a chronic condition at home.

children.text: Population health management requires three things fee-for-service practices rarely had: data, staff, and proactive processes. The data comes from electronic health records and claims. The staff — care managers or medical assistants in expanded roles — conduct outreach to patients who need follow-up. The processes include monthly panel reviews, risk stratification algorithms, and care gap closure protocols.

sanityBody.title: Population Health by the Numbers

stats.label: Patients Drive 50% of Costs
stats.context: Consistently, the sickest 5% of patients account for roughly 50% of total healthcare spending. VBC practices identify and intensively manage this group. Source: AHRQ.

stats.label: Chronic Disease Is Preventable
stats.context: The CDC estimates that 70% of chronic disease burden is preventable through lifestyle changes and early intervention — exactly what population health management targets.

stats.label: Impact of Care Management
stats.context: Patients enrolled in structured care management programs have 3x better adherence to treatment plans and significantly fewer ED visits. Source: Health Affairs, 2022.

children.text: Risk stratification is the engine of population health management. Practices use algorithms — built into EHR systems or analytics platforms — to sort patients into tiers based on their likelihood of a high-cost clinical event in the next 6 to 12 months. High-risk patients get intensive care management: regular check-ins, home visits, medication reconciliation. Low-risk patients get preventive outreach: reminders for annual wellness visits and screenings.

sanityBody.title: ChenMed — Intensive Primary Care for High-Risk Seniors
sanityBody.body: ChenMed operates primary care clinics specifically designed for high-risk Medicare patients. Their model flips the standard formula: instead of seeing 24 patients per day in 15-minute slots, ChenMed physicians see 8 to 10 patients per day for 40-minute visits. Every patient has a dedicated care team. Transportation to appointments is provided. Patients receive monthly wellness visits even when they are feeling fine.
sanityBody.outcome: ChenMed patients have 30 to 40 percent fewer hospitalizations and emergency department visits than matched comparison groups. Source: Health Affairs, 2020.
sanityBody.source: Health Affairs, 2020; ChenMed internal outcomes reporting

children.text: Care Coordination: The Connective Tissue of Value-Based Care

The US healthcare system was built around specialization. Cardiologists manage hearts. Endocrinologists manage diabetes. Orthopedic surgeons manage joints. This works extraordinarily well for complex procedures and rare conditions. It works catastrophically poorly for the average Medicare patient with five chronic conditions who sees seven different specialists — none of whom talk to each other.

Care Coordination: The deliberate organization of patient care activities and the sharing of information among all participants to achieve safer, more effective care. It includes communication between providers, follow-up after transitions, medication reconciliation, and ensuring patients understand their care plan.

Poor care coordination is expensive and dangerous. When a cardiologist adds a new medication and does not know the patient's nephrologist recently changed a kidney medication, the combination can cause serious harm. When a hospital discharges a patient with instructions to 'schedule a follow-up within a week' but does not help make that appointment, the patient often does not go — and ends up back in the ER within 30 days.

sanityBody.title: The Cost of Poor Care Coordination

stats.label: Annual Coordination Failure Cost
stats.context: Poor coordination — duplicated tests, medication errors, missed follow-ups — costs the US an estimated $27.2 billion annually. Source: Annals of Internal Medicine.

stats.label: Adults with Multiple Chronic Conditions
stats.context: More than half of US adults have at least 2 chronic conditions, requiring active coordination among multiple providers. Source: CDC, 2023.

stats.label: Patients Experience Coordination Failures
stats.context: One in three patients reports experiencing at least one care coordination problem in the past two years. Source: Commonwealth Fund 2022 International Health Policy Survey.

children.text: Value-based care fixes this by making coordination an explicit responsibility with a named owner. The care coordinator — often a registered nurse, social worker, or medical assistant in an extended role — serves as the connective tissue between providers, between hospital and home, and between patient and care plan. Their job is to make sure nothing falls through the cracks.

sanityBody.title: What a Care Coordinator Does in a VBC Practice

steps.title: Panel Review
steps.description: Weekly review of the patient panel with the care team. Flag patients overdue for follow-up, those who had a recent hospitalization, or whose risk score changed in the EHR. Decide who gets a proactive outreach call this week.

steps.title: Transition Management
steps.description: When a patient is discharged from the hospital, the coordinator calls within 48 to 72 hours: Did you fill your medications? Do you understand your discharge instructions? Is your follow-up appointment scheduled? Can you get there?

steps.title: Specialist Coordination
steps.description: Ensure that specialist visit notes are shared with the primary care team. Follow up to confirm referrals were completed. Flag conflicting medication orders for physician review.

steps.title: Medication Reconciliation
steps.description: At every transition point — admission, discharge, specialist visit — reconcile the patient's complete medication list. Polypharmacy is a leading cause of preventable harm, especially in older adults.

steps.title: Patient Activation
steps.description: Help patients understand their care plan, set personal health goals, and navigate the health system. Activated patients — those who feel confident managing their own health — have significantly better outcomes and lower costs.

sanityBody.title: Vermont Blueprint for Health — Community Health Teams
sanityBody.body: Vermont's Blueprint for Health embeds Community Health Teams in primary care practices across the state. Each CHT includes nurses, social workers, dietitians, and community health workers co-located with or closely partnered with primary care practices. When a practice flags a high-risk patient — perhaps a diabetic with three recent ER visits — the CHT mobilizes. They assess barriers such as no transportation, food insecurity, or depression, connect patients to community resources, and manage follow-up.
sanityBody.outcome: Blueprint practices with active CHT partnerships have shown significant reductions in preventable hospitalization rates and improvements in chronic disease management scores compared to non-Blueprint practices. Source: Vermont DVHA Blueprint evaluation reports.
sanityBody.source: Vermont Department of Vermont Health Access, Blueprint for Health Annual Reports

children.text: Reducing Preventable Hospitalizations and Readmissions

Hospitalizations are the single largest driver of healthcare costs. A single inpatient stay for a Medicare patient costs, on average, more than $13,000. Many of those hospitalizations are for conditions that, if managed properly in an outpatient setting, should never have required a hospital bed. These are called ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — uncontrolled diabetes, COPD exacerbations, congestive heart failure, urinary tract infections.

Ambulatory Care-Sensitive Conditions (ACSCs): Medical conditions for which timely and appropriate outpatient care can prevent hospitalization. They include asthma, COPD, congestive heart failure, diabetes complications, and hypertension. High ACSC hospitalization rates signal that primary care access or quality is failing.

Value-based care contracts explicitly target ACSC hospitalization rates as a key performance indicator. A practice with a high ACSC rate is leaving money on the table — and more importantly, leaving patients in harm's way. Hospitalizations carry real clinical risk: hospital-acquired infections, medication errors, delirium in elderly patients, and the deconditioning from days of bed rest.

sanityBody.misconception: Keeping patients out of the hospital means denying them care they need.
sanityBody.reality: Reducing avoidable hospitalizations is about providing better care earlier — not rationing. A patient with COPD who sees their care coordinator monthly, has a written action plan for exacerbations, and can reach a nurse by phone when their breathing worsens is receiving better care than a patient who sees their doctor twice a year and lands in the hospital every winter. The goal is the right care in the right setting.

children.text: Readmissions are a related but distinct problem. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of discharge. The national Medicare readmission rate hovers around 15 to 20 percent. CMS began financially penalizing hospitals for excess readmissions in 2013 under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program. Since then, rates have declined — but remain stubbornly high.

sanityBody.title: Evidence-Based Interventions That Reduce Readmissions

steps.title: Structured Discharge Planning
steps.description: Use a standardized discharge checklist: review medications, schedule follow-up before discharge, provide written instructions in plain language at a 6th-grade reading level, confirm patient understanding via teach-back method.

steps.title: 48 to 72 Hour Post-Discharge Call
steps.description: A nurse or care coordinator calls within 2 to 3 days of discharge. Confirm the patient is taking medications correctly, understands warning signs, and has a follow-up appointment. Early problem identification prevents crisis.

steps.title: Rapid Follow-Up Appointment
steps.description: Patients seen by their primary care provider within 7 days of discharge have significantly lower readmission rates. Schedule this before the patient leaves the hospital whenever possible.

steps.title: Medication Reconciliation
steps.description: Medication errors during care transitions are extremely common. Pharmacist-led or nurse-led reconciliation at discharge — comparing the inpatient list to what the patient took before admission — catches dangerous discrepancies.

steps.title: Address Social Needs
steps.description: Many readmissions are driven by social factors: no food at home, no transportation to the pharmacy, social isolation causing non-adherence. Transitional care programs that screen for social needs and connect patients to community resources see the largest readmission reductions.

sanityBody.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has not been seen in your practice in 14 months. Her last HbA1c was 9.2 — well above the target of 8.0. She is not scheduled for an upcoming appointment. Under a value-based care contract, what should happen?
sanityBody.hint: Think about what 'population health management' means — and who is responsible for patients who are NOT in the office.
sanityBody.answer: Under a VBC contract, this patient represents an open care gap. The practice is responsible for her health outcomes even when she is not actively seeking care. The right response is proactive outreach: a care coordinator calls or sends a letter, offers scheduling assistance including transportation help if needed, and flags her for the team's panel review. If she has barriers to care — cost, transportation, work schedule — the team works to address them. Waiting for her to call is no longer acceptable practice.

children.text: The New Clinical Team: Roles That Value-Based Care Built

Value-based care has not replaced physicians. But it has radically expanded the clinical team around them. In a well-functioning VBC practice, the physician is the expert clinician and diagnostic mind — supported by a team that handles much of what was once shoved into a 15-minute visit or never done at all.

sanityBody.title: The Care Team: Traditional vs. Value-Based

rows.right: Physician, APP, RN care manager, care coordinator, social worker, CHW

rows.left: Patient calls us when something is wrong
rows.right: We proactively call patients between visits
Panel management reports, daily risk score reviews, care gap dashboards
Nurse triage line, telehealth, after-hours urgent access
