rows.right: Embedded behavioral health in primary care — same-day or next-day

children.text: Advanced Practice Providers — nurse practitioners and physician assistants — play an expanded role in VBC models, often managing the bulk of stable chronic disease visits and wellness exams while physicians focus on complex diagnostic cases. This is team-based care: the right person, for the right patient, at the right time.
Vermont Clinical Programs: Value-Based Care in Action

Vermont is not just talking about value-based clinical care — it has been running the experiment for over a decade. The Blueprint for Health, launched in 2006, was one of the first statewide primary care transformation programs in the country. Every participating practice has undergone a formal practice transformation process: team-based care, patient registries, care coordination, and quality measurement.

Vermont's All-Payer Model, which launched in 2017 and runs through 2029, takes this further. OneCare Vermont — the state's accountable care organization — holds a global budget covering roughly a third of Vermont residents. Practices within OneCare are responsible for the total cost of care for their attributed population. Every preventable hospitalization and readmission is a financial signal that something in the clinical model needs to change.

sanityBody.title: Copley Hospital — Rural VBC in Morrisville, Vermont
sanityBody.body: Copley Hospital is a 25-bed critical access hospital in Morrisville serving a largely rural population. As a member of OneCare Vermont, Copley participates in population health management for its attributed patients. The hospital invested in a care transition program: every patient discharged is followed by a registered nurse for 30 days post-discharge, and a risk stratification tool identifies patients most likely to be readmitted for intensified outreach.
sanityBody.outcome: Copley has maintained readmission rates well below state and national averages for a hospital serving a comparably complex patient population — demonstrating that rural hospitals can achieve VBC goals with the right team structure.
sanityBody.source: Vermont DVHA All-Payer Model evaluation, OneCare Vermont reporting

children.text: The Clinical Case for Value-Based Care

For many clinicians, the shift to value-based care feels like an administrative imposition — more metrics to track, more documentation requirements, more meetings. That is a legitimate concern, and it reflects real transition pain. But the underlying logic of VBC aligns more closely with why most clinicians entered medicine than fee-for-service ever did.

Fee-for-service rewarded doing more. It paid well for procedures and poorly for conversations, care coordination, and prevention. It created a system where a physician who spent 45 minutes with a complex elderly patient on 12 medications was paid the same as a physician who spent 10 minutes. It created burnout among clinicians who wanted to practice relationship-based medicine but were trapped on a volume treadmill.

Physician burnout is at crisis levels: 63% of physicians report burnout symptoms, with administrative burden and loss of clinical autonomy cited as primary drivers. VBC, done well, can restore what drew clinicians to medicine: time with patients, team support, and a payment system that rewards doing what is actually right for the patient. Source: AMA National Burnout Survey, 2025.

sanityBody.question: What is the difference between a 'preventable hospitalization' and a '30-day readmission,' and why do both matter under VBC contracts?
sanityBody.hint: Think about timing — one happens before the hospital stay, one happens after.
sanityBody.answer: A preventable hospitalization (ambulatory care-sensitive admission) is a hospital stay that could have been avoided with timely outpatient care — like a COPD patient hospitalized for an exacerbation that could have been managed in the clinic with proper monitoring and medication adjustment. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of being discharged. Both matter under VBC because they represent clinical failures where the care system fell short. Both carry financial consequences: preventable admissions represent waste, and readmissions trigger CMS penalties under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program.

sanityBody.title: Key Takeaways — Clinical Practice Under Value-Based Care
points: Fee-for-service pays for volume; value-based care pays for outcomes — this distinction reshapes every clinical workflow.
Quality measures in VBC track preventive care, chronic disease management, patient experience, and avoidable utilization.
Population health management means taking responsibility for patients who are NOT in the office — not just those who show up.
Care coordination is a clinical skill and a team function — it prevents the gaps between providers that cause harm and cost.
Preventable hospitalizations and readmissions are the most visible signals of clinical model failure — and the primary financial targets in VBC contracts.
Vermont's Blueprint for Health and All-Payer Model demonstrate that statewide clinical transformation is achievable with measurable results.
Value-based care, done well, can restore the relationship-centered practice that most clinicians entered medicine to provide.

lessons.title: Who Gets Left Behind: Health Equity, Social Determinants, and Building a VBC System That Works for Everyone
lessons.summary: Value-based care was designed, in part, as a health equity intervention — rewarding good outcomes rather than high volume should help the patients who need the most help. But the research tells a more complicated story. This module examines where VBC has advanced health equity, where it has undermined it, and what specific design choices — in risk adjustment, community health worker programs, panel selection, and rural policy — are required to build a VBC system that actually works for everyone.

objectives.text: Define health disparities and social determinants of health using current data
Explain three structural equity flaws in how most VBC programs are currently designed
Describe how SDOH risk adjustment works and why the current CMS approach is considered insufficient
Explain the evidence base for community health workers and the reimbursement barriers they face
Identify Vermont-specific equity challenges including rural, refugee, and indigenous populations
Describe what equity-centered VBC design requires beyond good intentions

children.text: In 2019, a landmark study published in the journal Science made a startling discovery. A widely used commercial algorithm — the kind that decides which patients get enrolled in intensive care management programs — was systematically underestimating the health needs of Black patients. Not by a little. The algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were, on average, significantly healthier. The practical consequence: Black patients were less likely to be identified for the high-intensity care management they needed.

This module is the culmination of the course — and arguably its most important chapter. Value-based care promises to improve health for everyone by aligning incentives with outcomes rather than volume. But a payment reform that perpetuates or amplifies existing health inequities is not a solution. It is a new version of the same problem. Understanding where VBC fails on equity — and how to fix it — is not optional knowledge for healthcare leaders. It is the central challenge of our generation.
What Health Disparities Actually Look Like

A health disparity is a difference in health outcomes between population groups that is preventable, avoidable, and unjust. It is not just the observation that some groups are sicker than others — it is the recognition that those differences are not random. They reflect systematic disadvantages in access to healthcare, economic stability, education, safe housing, and healthy food.

Health Disparity: A preventable difference in the burden of disease, injury, violence, or opportunity to achieve optimal health between groups defined by race, ethnicity, income, education, disability, geography, or other social characteristics.

sanityBody.title: Health Disparities in the United States

stats.label: Black-White Life Expectancy Gap
stats.context: Black Americans live 3.5 fewer years on average than white Americans. The gap widened to 6 years during COVID-19 due to disparate mortality rates. Source: CDC National Vital Statistics, 2023.

stats.label: Maternal Mortality: Black vs. White
stats.context: Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at more than twice the rate of white women — even after controlling for income and education. Source: CDC, 2023.

stats.label: Rural vs. Urban Mortality Gap
stats.context: Rural Americans have age-adjusted mortality rates 20% higher than urban Americans — a gap that has widened over the past two decades as rural hospital closures and provider shortages compound. Source: JAMA, 2024.

children.text: These disparities are not primarily explained by genetic differences or individual health behaviors. The research literature is clear: the most powerful predictors of health outcomes are social and economic — where you live, what you earn, whether your neighborhood has a grocery store, whether you can take a day off work to see a doctor. These are the social determinants of health.
Social Determinants of Health: The 30 to 55 Percent of Outcomes We Rarely Treat

Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age that shape health outcomes. They include: income and wealth, educational attainment, employment quality, food security, housing stability and quality, transportation access, neighborhood safety, and social connectedness. The evidence that SDOH factors account for 30 to 55 percent of health outcome variation — compared to only 10 to 20 percent typically attributed to clinical care — is now firmly established in the research literature.

sanityBody.analogy: Imagine a leaky pipe in an apartment building. You can hire the best plumber in the city to mop up the water every day — and they will do excellent work. But if you never fix the pipe, the water keeps coming. Clinical care is the mopping. Social determinants are the pipe.
sanityBody.bridge: We spend enormous resources on excellent clinical care — the mopping — while chronically under-investing in the conditions that cause people to get sick in the first place. Value-based care, when designed well, starts asking about the pipe: it screens for food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers, and connects patients to resources that address those root causes.

children.text: The most frequently screened SDOH domains in clinical settings are food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers, social isolation, interpersonal violence, and low health literacy. Standardized screening tools — including the Accountable Health Communities tool and the PRAPARE instrument — allow clinical teams to systematically identify SDOH needs during routine visits. But screening alone is insufficient. The critical next step — connecting patients to community resources that address those needs — is where most health systems still struggle.

sanityBody.title: Social Determinants in VBC Populations

stats.label: Food Insecurity Prevalence
stats.context: 34% of high-risk VBC patients screen positive for food insecurity. Food-insecure patients have a 2.1x higher risk of preventable hospitalization. Source: AHRQ, 2024.

stats.label: Transportation Barriers
stats.context: 29% of high-risk VBC patients report transportation barriers to care. Missing appointments due to lack of transportation drives medication non-adherence and delayed diagnosis. Source: AHRQ, 2024.

stats.label: Housing Instability Risk Multiplier
stats.context: Patients experiencing housing instability or homelessness have 4.2x higher risk of preventable hospitalization than stably housed patients. Source: NEJM, 2023.

children.text: Three Structural Equity Flaws in Current VBC Design

Value-based care was intended to be an equity intervention — aligning incentives with population health outcomes should, in theory, help the patients who need the most help. The reality is more complicated. Three structural equity problems have been consistently documented in the VBC research literature. Understanding all three is essential for any leader who wants to build VBC programs that advance rather than undermine health equity.

sanityBody.title: Three Structural Equity Flaws in VBC

steps.title: The Panel Selection Problem
steps.description: Under most ACO attribution rules, providers who serve the most medically and socially complex patients will systematically generate worse performance on standard quality metrics — not because they deliver worse care, but because their patients face compounding barriers outside clinical control. This creates financial pressure to avoid accepting the most vulnerable patients, which is precisely the opposite of what VBC should incentivize.

steps.title: The Metric Design Problem
steps.description: Standard VBC quality metrics do not adequately account for the social determinants of health that drive 30 to 55 percent of outcome variation. A physician serving a food-insecure, transportation-poor population will show worse HbA1c control rates than a physician serving a food-secure, transportation-rich population — even if the former is a dramatically better clinician. Unadjusted metrics penalize providers for serving high-need populations.

steps.title: The Investment Allocation Problem
steps.description: The organizations with the greatest ability to invest in care management infrastructure — large health systems, well-capitalized ACOs, urban medical centers — are not the organizations serving the highest-need populations. Rural safety-net providers and Federally Qualified Health Centers serving predominantly low-income and minority populations often lack the capital to build the VBC infrastructure that would most benefit their patients.

children.text: The panel selection problem is the most empirically documented. A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients. The program's financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations.

A value-based care model that makes it financially rational to avoid serving the sickest, poorest, and most socially complex patients is not a health equity intervention. It is a health equity obstruction wearing the language of reform. Getting the incentives right requires explicit equity design — not just good intentions layered on top of metrics that were built for a different patient population.
SDOH Risk Adjustment: Making the Metrics Fair

The metric design problem — the failure of standard quality metrics to account for social determinants — is the most technically solvable of VBC's equity challenges. SDOH risk adjustment means modifying performance benchmarks to account for the social complexity of the patient population being served, so that providers are compared to peers serving similar populations rather than to the national average.

CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases spending benchmarks for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status. This acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively. However, the 3.5 percent adjustment ceiling is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers — and it uses low-income subsidy status as an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation.

children.text: CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors. These changes are meaningful but still incomplete. The policy change required to make VBC metrics truly equitable will require sustained advocacy from providers who are experiencing the consequences of inadequate adjustment directly.

sanityBody.misconception: If we improve clinical quality across the board, health disparities will naturally narrow.
sanityBody.reality: Research consistently shows that quality improvement programs that do not explicitly target disparities can widen them. When a health system improves its overall diabetes control rates, the improvement is often concentrated among the most engaged, most resource-rich patients — while the most vulnerable patients remain unchanged or worsen. Closing disparities requires measuring them separately, targeting interventions at high-disparity populations, and tracking equity-specific outcomes, not just aggregate averages.

children.text: Community Health Workers: The Most Powerful Equity Tool in VBC

Community health workers — frontline public health workers who are typically members of the communities they serve, with lived experience of the social and health challenges those communities face — are emerging as the most powerful equity tool in value-based care. Where clinical care coordinators manage disease processes and care transitions, CHWs address the social and environmental factors that determine whether clinical interventions succeed.

Community Health Worker (CHW): A frontline public health worker who is a trusted member of and has a close understanding of the community being served. CHWs serve as a bridge between health and social services and the communities they serve, reduce cultural and social barriers to care, and provide health education, advocacy, and social support in community settings. They are NOT case managers or care coordinators — the community trust and cultural competence that makes their work effective must be lived, not credentialed.

What makes CHWs distinctive — and irreplaceable — is trust. In communities that have historically had reason to distrust institutional medicine, a CHW who grew up in the neighborhood, speaks the language, and has navigated the same systems can accomplish what no clinical protocol can. They connect patients to food assistance programs, navigate housing resources, provide transportation to appointments, and serve as advocates within a healthcare system that can feel foreign and hostile to those who most need it.

sanityBody.title: The Evidence for Community Health Workers

stats.label: Reduction in Preventable Hospitalizations
stats.context: A 2024 meta-analysis of 47 RCTs found CHW programs targeting high-risk populations produced an average 22% reduction in preventable hospitalizations. Source: AJPH, 2024.

stats.label: CHW Return on Investment
stats.context: CHW programs consistently show a 4-to-1 return on investment — the highest ROI of any care management intervention type studied. Source: Health Affairs, 2023.

stats.label: Chronic Disease Monitoring Improvement
stats.context: CHW programs targeting high-risk populations show a 31% improvement in chronic disease monitoring completion rates — exceeding care coordinator programs alone. Source: AJPH, 2024.

children.text: Despite this evidence base, CHW integration into VBC programs has been slower than warranted, primarily because of reimbursement barriers. Most fee-for-service billing structures do not include a direct reimbursement pathway for CHW services, requiring VBC organizations to fund CHW positions out of shared savings or grants. This creates funding fragility — organizations that cannot sustain CHW positions between shared savings payments cycle through workforce disruption that undermines the relationship continuity that makes CHW programs effective.

CMS has taken meaningful steps to address this. The 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule created a federal minimum standard requiring all state Medicaid programs to provide reimbursement for defined CHW services by 2026. The AHEAD Model's health equity investment fund provides direct CHW program funding in participating states. Vermont, as an AHEAD participant, has an explicit CHW funding stream tied to the All-Payer Model performance requirements.

sanityBody.title: Roots Community Health Center — CHWs as Clinical Infrastructure
sanityBody.body: Roots Community Health Center in Oakland, California serves a predominantly Black and low-income patient population. Their CHW program places community health workers in every primary care team. CHWs conduct SDOH screenings, make home visits for high-risk patients, connect patients to food and housing resources, attend medical appointments as patient advocates, and provide health education in culturally relevant formats. CHWs are paid employees with full benefits — not volunteers or contractors — reflecting the organization's commitment to workforce stability.
sanityBody.outcome: Roots patients with CHW engagement have 40% lower preventable hospitalization rates than demographically matched patients in the surrounding area, and significantly higher rates of completing preventive screenings. Source: Roots Community Health Center outcome reporting, 2024.
sanityBody.source: Roots Community Health Center, UCSF Center for Excellence in Primary Care evaluation, 2024

children.text: Rural and Geographic Equity: The Invisible Disparity

Healthcare equity discussions in the United States have historically focused primarily on racial and ethnic disparities — and for important reasons. But a parallel geographic equity crisis receives far less policy attention: the systematic disadvantage faced by rural Americans in healthcare access, provider supply, and health outcomes relative to their urban peers.

Rural Americans are more likely to die from the five leading causes of preventable death — heart disease, cancer, unintentional injury, chronic lower respiratory disease, and stroke. They have fewer physicians per capita, longer travel distances to care, higher rates of uninsurance, and significantly lower rates of receiving recommended preventive services. And they are, as documented in the Technology module, disproportionately outside the VBC system entirely — receiving care under fee-for-service Medicare with its documented incentive failures.

sanityBody.title: Rural Health Equity Gaps

stats.label: Rural CAH Areas in MSSP ACOs
stats.context: Only 23% of rural Critical Access Hospital service areas are covered by an MSSP ACO, compared to 71% of urban hospital referral regions. Rural patients are disproportionately in fee-for-service. Source: CMS, 2025.

stats.label: Rural Hospital Closures Since 2010
stats.context: 138 rural hospitals have closed since 2010, leaving millions of rural Americans further from emergency, obstetric, and inpatient care. Source: Chartis Center for Rural Health, 2025.

stats.label: Rural Mental Health Provider Shortage
stats.context: 62% of rural counties have no psychiatrist — forcing rural residents to travel hours for mental health care or go without. Behavioral health comorbidities are a major driver of preventable hospitalizations. Source: HRSA, 2025.

children.text: Vermont's Equity Landscape: Progress and Persistent Gaps

Vermont's All-Payer Model includes an explicit health equity performance requirement — a condition not present in most VBC programs nationally. The AHEAD Model requires participating states to establish measurable health equity goals and report progress annually. Vermont's current equity focus areas include reducing rural-urban disparities in preventive care rates, improving mental health access in rural counties, and addressing the health needs of Vermont's growing refugee and immigrant populations.

Vermont's refugee and immigrant populations — concentrated primarily in Burlington, Winooski, and Rutland — face compounding health equity challenges: language barriers, cultural differences in health-seeking behavior, immigration status concerns, trauma histories from displacement and persecution, and limited familiarity with a healthcare system very different from those in their countries of origin. Vermont's Blueprint for Health has piloted culturally adapted CHW programs for refugee communities, but coverage remains incomplete.

Vermont's Abenaki and other indigenous communities face health disparities that reflect both geographic isolation and historical trauma with healthcare institutions. The legacy of forced assimilation, medical experimentation, and involuntary sterilization programs has created well-founded distrust of the healthcare system that no appointment reminder or care coordinator can overcome. Rebuilding trust with indigenous communities requires sustained, community-led engagement over years — not program cycles.

sanityBody.title: Vermont Department of Health — Racial and Ethnic Health Equity Dashboard
sanityBody.body: Vermont has invested in a public-facing health equity dashboard that disaggregates health outcome data by race, ethnicity, income, and geography — making disparities visible to policymakers, providers, and communities. The dashboard tracks preventable hospitalization rates, chronic disease control metrics, maternal and infant health outcomes, and behavioral health utilization by population group. Vermont is one of only a handful of states with this level of equity data transparency at the state level.
sanityBody.outcome: Vermont's equity dashboard has become a policy accountability tool — allowing advocates and legislators to track whether All-Payer Model investments are narrowing identified disparities, and to demand explanations when they are not. Source: Vermont Department of Health, Racial and Ethnic Health Equity Dashboard, 2025.

sanityBody.misconception: Our organization serves everyone equally — we do not have health disparities here.
sanityBody.reality: Every healthcare organization serves patients with different outcomes based on race, income, and geography. The question is not whether disparities exist — it is whether you have measured them. Organizations that only report aggregate quality performance systematically miss disparities that are present in the underlying data. If you have not disaggregated your quality metrics by race, ethnicity, and income, you do not know your equity performance. You know your average performance.

children.text: AI Bias in Risk Stratification: Technology as an Equity Threat

The 2019 Science study described at the opening of this module identified a mechanism that explains the algorithmic underestimation of Black patients' health needs: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need. Black patients historically had lower healthcare costs — not because they were healthier, but because structural barriers had historically limited their access to care. The algorithm encoded a history of discrimination as a measure of health. The practical consequence: Black patients were significantly less likely to be flagged for high-intensity care management programs.

This problem has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types. As AI-powered risk stratification tools become increasingly central to VBC care management, the equity risk posed by biased training data becomes increasingly urgent. A healthcare organization that deploys an AI risk model without auditing it for demographic performance disparities is potentially using technology to automate discrimination at scale.

Technology Governance Requirement: Any healthcare organization deploying an AI risk stratification tool in a VBC context has an ethical and, increasingly, a legal obligation to audit the tool for demographic performance disparities before deployment. The audit should examine whether the model's accuracy varies significantly across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups. If it does, the organization must select a different model, recalibrate it for its specific population, or supplement algorithmic scores with clinical and social worker judgment for populations where the algorithm performs poorly.
Building Equity-Centered VBC: What It Actually Takes

Building a VBC program that genuinely advances health equity rather than performing it in marketing materials requires design choices that are sometimes in tension with the financial optimization logic that drives most VBC strategy discussions. Equity-centered VBC design requires accepting lower short-term shared savings in exchange for serving populations whose care management needs are higher. It requires investing in CHW infrastructure before guaranteed funding arrives. It requires choosing quality metrics that are SDOH-adjusted rather than metrics that produce better scores simply because you serve a more advantaged population.

sanityBody.title: Five Concrete Steps Toward Equity-Centered VBC

steps.title: Implement Systematic SDOH Screening
steps.description: Adopt the CMS Accountable Health Communities screening tool or PRAPARE instrument as a standard clinical workflow for all attributed VBC patients. SDOH data that is not systematically collected cannot be incorporated into risk adjustment, care planning, or community investment decisions. Start with your highest-risk quartile and expand from there.

steps.title: Disaggregate Your Quality Metrics
steps.description: Disaggregate all quality metric performance data by race, ethnicity, income level, and geography before reporting aggregate performance. Organizations that only examine aggregate quality scores systematically miss equity disparities present in the underlying data — disparities that will worsen without targeted intervention.

steps.title: Audit Your Risk Stratification Algorithms
steps.description: If you use AI-powered risk stratification, conduct a demographic equity audit before the next contract cycle. Examine whether the model's accuracy varies by race, income, and geography. If it does, address it — through vendor recalibration, supplemental clinical judgment, or a different tool.

steps.title: Build a CHW Program Now
steps.description: The CHW ROI evidence and the 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule make 2026 the right year to build or expand a CHW program. Hire CHWs with lived experience of the specific communities and social challenges your highest-need patients face. Do not hire case managers and call them CHWs.

steps.title: Advocate for SDOH Risk Adjustment
steps.description: Advocate explicitly for SDOH risk adjustment in every VBC contract negotiation with payers and in every CMS rulemaking comment you submit. The policy change required to fix the metric design problem will not happen without sustained, evidence-based advocacy from providers who are experiencing its consequences directly.

sanityBody.question: A health system reports that its overall HbA1c control rate for diabetic patients has improved from 61% to 74% over three years — a significant achievement. Should leadership declare victory on diabetes equity?
sanityBody.hint: Think about what aggregate statistics can hide.
sanityBody.answer: Not without disaggregating the data. If the improvement was distributed equally across all demographic groups — white, Black, Latino, low-income, rural — then the organization has genuinely improved equity. But the research literature consistently shows that quality improvement programs that do not explicitly target disparate populations tend to improve aggregate rates by improving outcomes for the most engaged, most resource-rich patients while leaving the most vulnerable behind. If the system's HbA1c improvement was concentrated among higher-income, white patients while control rates for low-income Black and rural patients remained flat or worsened, the aggregate improvement actually reflects a widening disparity. The only way to know is to look at the disaggregated data — and report it publicly.

sanityBody.question: A community health worker in your organization reports that a risk stratification algorithm has been flagging very few Black patients on her panel for high-intensity care management — even patients she knows from clinical experience to be at high risk. What should she do, and what structural issue does this reflect?
sanityBody.hint: Think about the 2019 Science study and how AI models are trained.
sanityBody.answer: The CHW should escalate her observation to clinical and data analytics leadership as a potential algorithmic bias issue — this is exactly the kind of frontline signal that formal AI equity audits are designed to detect. The structural issue is that AI risk stratification models are trained on historical utilization data, and if Black patients in the training dataset historically had lower healthcare utilization due to access barriers — not because they were healthier — the model will have learned to associate lower utilization with lower risk, systematically underestimating the risk of Black patients. This is the bias mechanism identified in the 2019 Obermeyer et al. Science study. The organization should conduct a formal demographic equity audit of the algorithm and report findings to leadership. If the bias is confirmed, the tool must be recalibrated, replaced, or supplemented with clinical judgment for affected populations.

children.text: Course Conclusion: What Value-Based Care Can and Cannot Do

Across six modules, this course has examined value-based care through every lens that matters: the economic incentive logic that makes it necessary, the policy architecture that makes it operational, the economics that determine whether it saves money, the technology that makes it analytically possible, the clinical model that determines whether it actually improves patient outcomes, and the equity design requirements that determine whether it works for everyone. The honest conclusion is nuanced but ultimately optimistic.

Value-based care, when designed well, implemented with adequate infrastructure, and evaluated with appropriate equity metrics, produces meaningfully better clinical outcomes than fee-for-service at lower total cost. The fee-for-service system that currently dominates American healthcare is producing the worst outcomes per dollar of any wealthy nation on earth. The most credible available alternative — paying for health rather than for activity — is demonstrably capable of doing better.

What value-based care cannot do, on its own, is eliminate the social determinants of health that account for 30 to 55 percent of outcome variation. It cannot provide affordable housing, food security, safe neighborhoods, or living wages — the most powerful health interventions available at the population level. These are not arguments against value-based care. They are arguments for building it with sufficient ambition, equity intentionality, and long-term commitment to match the scale of the problem it is trying to solve.

Vermont's AHEAD Model participation is the most ambitious attempt in state history to align payment incentives, equity goals, and clinical infrastructure toward a single measurable objective: a healthier population at sustainable cost. Whether it succeeds will depend on the willingness of providers, payers, policymakers, and community organizations to make the hard design choices that equity-centered VBC requires.

sanityBody.title: Key Takeaways — Health Equity and Value-Based Care
points: Health disparities are preventable differences in outcomes between population groups — driven primarily by social determinants, not genetics or individual behavior.
Social determinants of health account for 30 to 55 percent of health outcome variation, yet remain largely outside clinical care delivery.
Three structural equity flaws in current VBC design: the panel selection problem, the metric design problem, and the investment allocation problem.
SDOH risk adjustment is the technical fix for inequitable quality metrics — but the current CMS adjustment is insufficient in magnitude and scope.
Community health workers are the most powerful equity tool in VBC, with a 4-to-1 ROI and 22% reduction in preventable hospitalizations in high-need populations.
AI risk stratification tools can encode and automate historical discrimination — demographic equity audits before deployment are ethically and increasingly legally required.
Disaggregating quality metrics by race, income, and geography is not optional — aggregate improvement can mask widening disparities beneath the average.
Vermont's AHEAD Model equity requirements represent the most ambitious state-level commitment to equity-centered VBC in the country — and a national model worth watching.

lessons.title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 2: The Policy Pillar — Laws, Rules, and the Regulatory Architecture That Makes (or Breaks) Value-Based Care
lessons.summary: Module 2 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the federal and state policy architecture that governs value-based care adoption in the United States. Building on Module 1’s conceptual foundation, this module explains in plain language how MACRA, the ACA’s Innovation Center, and state Medicaid waiver programs create the legal and financial scaffolding for VBC models, identifies the regulatory barriers that slow adoption for rural and safety-net providers, and equips learners to read and interpret the policy signals that will shape their organization’s VBC strategy through 2030. No prior policy or legal background is required.

objectives.text: Explain MACRA's two-track physician payment architecture and the financial difference between MIPS and Advanced APM participation.
Describe how the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions enable ACO-physician financial arrangements.
Identify the policy signals — RFIs, fee schedule proposed rules, model termination notices — that indicate future VBC direction.
Compare state Medicaid VBC adoption using Section 1115 and 1915 waiver frameworks.
Summarize the AHEAD Model's all-payer structure and explain why it is architecturally different from single-payer VBC models.

children.text: Imagine you want to start a new kind of restaurant — one that charges customers a flat monthly fee to eat as many healthy meals as they need, rather than charging per dish. The idea makes sense nutritionally and economically. But before you open, you discover that local zoning laws require all food establishments to post per-item prices. The health department’s inspection checklist was designed for traditional menus. Your liquor license application has no category for subscription dining. None of these rules were written to block your idea — they were simply written when your idea did not exist. This is precisely the situation that value-based care innovators face in the American healthcare regulatory environment. The laws, billing codes, anti-kickback rules, and licensure frameworks that govern U.S. healthcare were almost entirely written for a fee-for-service world. Navigating, modifying, and sometimes working around them is not a bureaucratic inconvenience for VBC implementation — it is one of its defining challenges.
Why Policy Is a Pillar, Not Just a Background Condition

Healthcare is one of the most heavily regulated industries in the United States, and for good reason: the decisions made in healthcare settings involve life and death, profound information asymmetry between providers and patients, and the expenditure of trillions of dollars of public funds. The regulatory architecture that governs healthcare payment — Medicare and Medicaid rules, anti-kickback statutes, the Stark Law governing physician self-referral, state insurance laws, and HIPAA privacy regulations — was built incrementally over six decades, each layer added in response to a specific problem or abuse. The result is a regulatory environment of extraordinary complexity that can simultaneously protect patients and obstruct innovation, often in the same rule. For value-based care specifically, the policy environment matters in three distinct ways: it determines which VBC models are legally permissible, it shapes the financial terms under which VBC contracts can operate, and it establishes the data sharing authorities that VBC’s information infrastructure depends upon.

The good news for learners approaching this material is that you do not need to become a healthcare attorney to understand the policy landscape for VBC. What you do need is a working knowledge of four things: the major federal legislation that authorized and funds VBC programs, the agency — CMS and its Innovation Center — that designs and operates most federal VBC models, the specific legal waivers that allow VBC arrangements to operate outside standard fee-for-service rules, and the state-level Medicaid policy environment that governs VBC adoption for the Medicaid population, which represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending and the majority of payer mix for rural and safety-net hospitals. This module covers all four in sequence, with enough practical depth that you can apply the concepts to your organization’s specific situation.
The ACA’s Innovation Center: The Engine of U.S. VBC Development

The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, universally known as CMMI, was established by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a mandatory appropriation of $10 billion over ten years and a statutory mission to test, evaluate, and scale new payment and delivery models that reduce spending while preserving or improving quality. CMMI’s legal authority is significant: it can implement new payment models for Medicare and Medicaid without going through the standard notice-and-comment rulemaking process that governs most federal regulation, as long as the model operates within specific statutory parameters and is evaluated by CMS’s Office of the Actuary. This streamlined authority was deliberately designed to allow rapid policy experimentation — the legislative drafters recognized that VBC model design requires iteration and learning, and that subjecting every model modification to a 12-month rulemaking cycle would make meaningful innovation impossible.

Since 2011, CMMI has launched more than 50 distinct payment model pilots across Medicare and Medicaid, covering primary care transformation, specialty care bundling, accountable care organizations, direct contracting, and state-level all-payer models. The budget allocated per model varies enormously — from small demonstration projects covering a few thousand beneficiaries to large-scale national programs like the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which enrolled 11.2 million beneficiaries by 2025. CMMI’s mandate requires it to demonstrate that each model either reduces net Medicare spending, improves quality without increasing spending, or both. Models that fail to meet these thresholds are terminated. As of 2025, CMMI has terminated 14 models for insufficient evidence of savings or quality improvement, a track record that reflects honest evaluation but has also generated criticism from providers who invested substantially in model infrastructure before termination decisions.

CMMI’s authority to move faster than the standard rulemaking process is its most valuable feature and its most politically contested one. Every model CMMI launches is a hypothesis about how to organize care better. Some hypotheses are wrong. The question is whether the system is learning fast enough from both successes and failures. — Dr. Rahul Rajkumar, former CMMI Deputy Director, Health Affairs Blog, 2024.
MACRA: The Law That Made VBC Participation Effectively Mandatory for Physicians

If CMMI is the engine of federal VBC development, the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 — universally known as MACRA — is the law that turned VBC from an optional experiment into the default trajectory for physician payment in Medicare. MACRA was passed with rare bipartisan consensus, repealing the deeply unpopular Sustainable Growth Rate formula that had governed Medicare physician payments since 1997 and replacing it with a two-track system that explicitly links physician payment updates to VBC participation. Understanding MACRA’s structure is essential for any clinical or administrative leader whose organization bills Medicare for physician services, because it directly determines how physicians are paid and how much.

MACRA’s two tracks work as follows. Physicians who remain in traditional fee-for-service Medicare participate in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System, or MIPS, which adjusts their annual Medicare payments up or down by up to 9% based on performance across four categories: quality (45% weight), promoting interoperability (25%), improvement activities (15%), and cost (15%). MIPS is designed as a transitional step — it maintains the fee-for-service base payment structure while adding a performance overlay that rewards quality and penalizes inefficiency. The alternative track, and the one that MACRA’s architects intended as the destination, is participation in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model, or APM, which includes CMS-approved VBC arrangements that meet specific risk and quality criteria. Physicians who generate a sufficient share of their Medicare revenue through APM participation receive a 5% lump-sum bonus payment and are exempt from MIPS reporting requirements — a substantial financial incentive to move toward more advanced VBC structures.
The MIPS-to-APM Progression: What It Looks Like in Practice

The practical effect of MACRA’s two-track architecture is to create a structured pathway from fee-for-service through MIPS participation toward Advanced APM engagement, with financial incentives escalating at each stage. A solo primary care physician in rural Wyoming who bills Medicare exclusively on a fee-for-service basis is automatically enrolled in MIPS and will receive payment adjustments — upward or downward — based on their quality reporting, EHR utilization, and cost performance. The same physician who joins a CMMI-approved Accountable Care Organization and generates 50% of their Medicare revenue through that ACO qualifies as an Advanced APM participant, receives the 5% bonus, and escapes the MIPS reporting burden. MACRA’s architecture was designed to make this progression financially attractive enough that providers would voluntarily move toward advanced VBC structures over time, without the political controversy of making VBC participation legally mandatory.

children.text: Policy Insight for Practice Leaders: If your organization’s physicians are currently in MIPS and scoring below 75, you are almost certainly paying more in administrative reporting costs than you are receiving in payment bonuses. The CMS data consistently shows that the cost of MIPS compliance for small and independent practices averages $12,800 per physician per year in staff time and technology costs. Joining an ACO or Advanced APM eliminates this burden while generating shared savings upside. The question is not whether to make the move — it is when your organization has the infrastructure to do it responsibly.
The Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute: The Rules VBC Had to Work Around

Two of the most significant legal barriers to value-based care adoption are laws that were designed to protect patients from fraud: the Stark Law, which prohibits physician self-referral for designated health services when a financial relationship exists between the physician and the referred entity, and the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute, which prohibits offering or receiving anything of value to induce referrals of federal healthcare program business. Both laws were enacted in the 1980s and 1990s to address genuine abuses in fee-for-service medicine — physicians referring patients to laboratories or imaging centers they owned, and pharmaceutical companies paying physicians to prescribe specific drugs. They are important protections. They are also written in a way that, on their face, makes many value-based care arrangements technically illegal.

Consider a simple VBC arrangement: a hospital wants to share a portion of the savings generated by an ACO with the primary care physicians who successfully manage their attributed patient panels and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations. Under a strict reading of the Anti-Kickback Statute, this payment could be characterized as remuneration to physicians for reducing referrals to the hospital — which is exactly what the statute was written to prohibit when the financial relationship runs in the other direction. In November 2020, CMS and the Department of Justice’s Office of Inspector General simultaneously published new rules — commonly called the Stark Law and AKS VBC Exceptions — that created explicit regulatory safe harbors for value-based arrangements meeting specific criteria. These exceptions are the legal foundation on which most current VBC contract structures rest, and understanding their existence (if not their full technical detail) is important context for any leader involved in VBC contract negotiation.
What the 2020 VBC Exceptions Actually Allow

The 2020 Stark Law and AKS VBC exceptions created three tiers of safe harbor protection based on the level of financial risk the arrangement assumes. The first tier, the “care coordination arrangement” exception, covers low-risk VBC arrangements where physicians and hospitals share non-monetary resources — care coordinators, technology platforms, data analytics tools — without direct financial remuneration flowing between them. The second tier covers arrangements where the parties share substantial downside financial risk, defined as the physician group being responsible for a meaningful share of losses if spending targets are not met. The third and most protective tier applies to arrangements where a physician entity is “fully at risk” — accepting capitation-level accountability for a defined patient population. The practical effect of this tiered structure is that more financially protective exceptions are available to VBC arrangements that accept more financial risk — a policy design that explicitly incentivizes providers to move toward more advanced VBC models in exchange for greater legal certainty.
State Medicaid Policy: Where VBC Gets Complicated Fast

Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for low-income Americans, covers 90 million people and represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending. For rural and safety-net hospitals, Medicaid is often the dominant payer — in some Critical Access Hospitals, Medicaid accounts for more than 40% of patient volume. Any serious discussion of VBC adoption must therefore grapple with Medicaid policy, and Medicaid policy is, by design, a state-level affair. Under the Social Security Act, the federal government sets minimum Medicaid standards and matches state spending at rates ranging from 50% to 90% depending on state per-capita income — but states have substantial flexibility in how they design their Medicaid programs, including how they pay providers. This flexibility has produced a 50-state patchwork of Medicaid VBC approaches that range from nationally leading to years behind, often with little correlation to state wealth or healthcare system capacity.

States access this flexibility primarily through two mechanisms: Section 1115 waivers, which allow states to use Medicaid funds in ways not otherwise permitted by federal statute in exchange for CMS approval of a formal waiver application and evaluation framework, and Section 1915 waivers, which allow states to require Medicaid beneficiaries to enroll in managed care organizations rather than traditional fee-for-service Medicaid. As of 2025, 41 states operate Medicaid managed care programs covering at least some beneficiary populations, and 24 states have active Section 1115 waivers that include VBC-oriented payment reform components. The remaining states continue to operate primarily fee-for-service Medicaid programs, creating a two-tier national Medicaid environment where the VBC infrastructure, data systems, and provider capabilities in a given state depend heavily on decisions made by state legislatures and Medicaid agencies that most healthcare professionals are only vaguely aware of.

children.text: The state variation in Medicaid VBC adoption documented in the table above is not simply a story of some states moving faster than others. It reflects fundamentally different political economies, administrative capacities, and provider infrastructure realities. Massachusetts’ MassHealth ACO Program, which places 78% of Medicaid beneficiaries in global budget arrangements, required a decade of incremental managed care development, a sophisticated state health information exchange, and a robust community health worker infrastructure before global budgets were feasible. Mississippi, which remains 89% fee-for-service Medicaid, faces not just a political environment less favorable to managed care but a provider infrastructure so financially fragile — as examined in the DSH module — that asking rural hospitals to accept downside financial risk before their basic solvency is secured would be policy malpractice. Understanding this context prevents the common mistake of treating state VBC laggards as simply lacking political will, when the more accurate diagnosis is often a missing infrastructure foundation.
The AHEAD Model: The Boldest Current Federal VBC Policy Experiment

The CMS All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model, known as AHEAD, launched in 2023 and represents the most ambitious federal VBC policy experiment currently active in the United States. AHEAD is fundamentally different from previous CMS models in one critical way: it operates across all payers simultaneously, not just Medicare. In the eight participating states — Maryland, Vermont, Connecticut, Hawaii, Minnesota, New York, Rhode Island, and Washington — CMS is working with state governments and commercial insurers to establish coordinated spending targets that apply to Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance simultaneously. The goal is to eliminate the perverse incentive created by single-payer VBC models, where a provider that successfully reduces costs for its Medicare ACO population may simply shift utilization to its commercially insured population, producing savings for Medicare at the expense of commercial payer spending.

AHEAD’s architecture has three components that build on each other. Hospital Global Budgets establish annual spending targets for inpatient and outpatient hospital care, similar to the model Maryland has operated since 1977 under a waiver from standard Medicare payment rules. Primary Care Investment establishes a per-capita funding floor for primary care services in each participating state, addressing the underfunding of primary care that Module 1 identified as a structural driver of the U.S. spending-outcomes gap. And the Health Equity Plan requires each participating state to establish specific, measurable goals for reducing health outcome disparities across racial, ethnic, geographic, and socioeconomic dimensions, with CMS oversight of progress toward those goals as a condition of continued model participation. AHEAD’s early results will not be statistically meaningful until 2027 at the earliest, but its structural design represents the most coherent attempt yet to address the whole-system payment reform that health economists have argued is necessary for genuine transformation.

The AHEAD Model is not a pilot. It is a policy architecture for what the American healthcare payment system could look like at scale — one where no payer is an island, where primary care is funded as infrastructure rather than as a commodity, and where health equity is a contractual obligation rather than an aspiration. Whether it works depends entirely on whether the participating states build the administrative and data infrastructure to make the targets meaningful. — HTR Regulatory Intelligence Assessment, Q1 2026.
Reading Policy Signals: How to Know What’s Coming Before It Arrives

One of the most practical skills a healthcare leader can develop is the ability to read federal policy signals early — to understand what CMS, Congress, and state Medicaid agencies are signaling about the future direction of payment policy before new rules take effect. This skill is valuable because VBC model participation requires organizational investment — in data systems, care management staffing, and actuarial capabilities — that takes 18 to 36 months to build. Organizations that wait until a rule is finalized to begin building readiness will always be behind. The following framework identifies the primary signals that healthcare leaders should monitor continuously as leading indicators of VBC policy direction.

CMS Requests for Information (RFIs) are formal public notices in which CMS invites stakeholder comment on a policy concept before publishing a proposed rule. An RFI on a new payment model concept typically precedes a proposed rule by 12–18 months, giving organizations that monitor them a substantial head start on understanding what is coming and beginning internal readiness assessments.

The Annual Physician Fee Schedule Proposed Rule, published every July for the following calendar year, contains the annual MIPS threshold adjustments, quality measure updates, and any modifications to Advanced APM qualifying criteria. Reading the proposed rule summary — not the full document, which runs to thousands of pages — each July is the single most efficient way to stay current on federal physician payment policy.

CMMI Model Termination Notices are official signals that a payment model has not met its statutory savings or quality thresholds. When CMMI terminates a model, it typically publishes evaluation findings that explain why. Reading these findings is often more instructive than reading the original model design documents, because they identify the specific infrastructure gaps, attribution problems, or market conditions that prevented the model from working — lessons directly applicable to understanding what makes other VBC models succeed.

State Medicaid Managed Care Request for Proposals are published by state Medicaid agencies when they are procuring new managed care contracts, typically on three-to-five year cycles. These documents specify the quality metrics, VBC incentive structures, SDOH screening requirements, and health equity goals that Medicaid managed care organizations and their provider networks will be held to. Organizations that serve Medicaid populations should read their state’s current managed care RFP as a direct statement of the performance expectations they will face in the next contract cycle.
Module 2 Summary: The Policy Environment Is Not Your Enemy — But You Must Understand It

The policy architecture governing value-based care in the United States is complex, layered, and still evolving — but it is not impenetrable to practitioners willing to invest in understanding its structure. The key institutions are CMS and its Innovation Center, which design and operate most federal VBC models; Congress, which authorizes and funds VBC infrastructure through legislation like MACRA and the ACA; and state Medicaid agencies, which determine how value-based principles are applied to the Medicaid population that drives solvency for most safety-net and rural providers. The key legal frameworks are MACRA’s two-track physician payment architecture, the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions, and the Section 1115 and 1915 waiver authorities that give states flexibility to innovate within federal Medicaid rules.

The most important single insight from this module is that policy does not just regulate VBC — it enables it. The shared savings that MSSP ACOs distribute to physicians are legal because of CMMI’s model authority and the AKS safe harbor. The global budgets that Maryland hospitals operate under are legal because of a 47-year-old CMS waiver. The care coordination resources that a hospital shares with its independent physician partners are legally protected because of the 2020 VBC exceptions. Every advanced VBC arrangement you will encounter in your career rests on a specific legal and regulatory foundation. Understanding that foundation — at least at the level of knowing which questions to ask your legal team — is not optional for any leader who wants to move their organization toward value.

Identify your organization’s current MACRA track: are your physicians primarily in MIPS, in an Advanced APM, or in both? If primarily MIPS, what is the organization’s target timeline for APM qualification, and what infrastructure gaps stand between you and that threshold?

Review your state’s current Medicaid managed care contract or RFP. Identify the three quality metrics with the highest incentive weight and assess your organization’s current performance on each. The gap between your current performance and the contract’s quality bonus threshold is a direct measure of revenue at risk.

Determine whether your state is an AHEAD Model participant. If yes, begin engaging your state hospital association and state health department about the hospital global budget timeline and what data your organization will need to submit. If no, monitor CMS for the next AHEAD cohort solicitation, expected in late 2026.

Schedule a conversation with your legal or compliance team specifically about the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions. Ask them to identify any current or planned VBC arrangements at your organization that rely on these exceptions, and to confirm that the arrangements are structured to satisfy the applicable safe harbor criteria.

Module 2 Key Takeaway: The U.S. healthcare policy environment was built for fee-for-service, but it has been systematically modified over the past 15 years to enable value-based care. CMMI’s model authority, MACRA’s APM incentive structure, the 2020 VBC legal exceptions, and state Medicaid waiver programs together constitute a policy architecture that makes advanced VBC legally and financially feasible for most U.S. healthcare organizations. The organizations that understand this architecture and align their strategy to it are the ones that will be best positioned as CMS accelerates its stated goal of having 100% of Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030.

lessons.title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 4: The Technology Pillar — Data, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure That Makes VBC Work
lessons.summary: Module 4 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the technology infrastructure that value-based care requires to function — and what happens when that infrastructure is missing. This module explains, in plain language, what interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and AI-powered risk stratification tools actually do in a VBC context, why 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals remain technology-unready for advanced VBC participation, and how the federal interoperability agenda — including the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability Rule, and the TEFCA framework — is building the data infrastructure that VBC depends upon. By the end of this module, learners will understand the specific technology capabilities that VBC models require, the sequence in which they should be built, and the federal programs that fund them.

objectives.text: Identify the three technology layers VBC requires and explain why each layer depends on the quality of the layer below it.
Describe what the 21st Century Cures Act's FHIR mandate and information blocking prohibition changed in health IT.
Explain how AI risk stratification improves on claims-based models and why demographic bias auditing is ethically required.
Assess an organization's VBC technology readiness using the rural-urban capability gap framework.
Apply the five-phase technology investment roadmap to prioritize VBC infrastructure investment sequentially.

children.text: Imagine trying to run a nationwide airline reservation system where every airport kept its flight records on paper, no two airports used the same form, and sharing records between airports required a fax machine and a three-day waiting period. Connecting passengers to flights would be technically possible but operationally chaotic — delays, lost records, missed connections, and dangerous errors would be routine, not exceptional. This is, only slightly exaggerated, the state of health information exchange in the United States as recently as 2019, and in many rural markets as recently as 2024. Value-based care requires something that American healthcare has never had at scale: a reliable, real-time, standards-based system for sharing patient health information across organizational boundaries. Without it, an Accountable Care Organization cannot know that its attributed Medicare patient was admitted to a hospital outside the network last Tuesday. A care coordinator cannot know that a high-risk patient missed their primary care appointment. A risk stratification algorithm cannot identify a patient approaching a high-cost event without complete longitudinal data about their diagnosis history, medication adherence, and recent utilization. Technology is not a nice-to-have for advanced VBC. It is the operating system on which the entire model runs.
The Three Technology Layers VBC Requires

The technology infrastructure that supports effective value-based care can be understood as three interdependent layers, each building on the one below it. The foundation layer is clinical data capture: the electronic health record system that documents every patient encounter, diagnosis, medication, order, and result in a structured, machine-readable format. The second layer is data integration and exchange: the health information exchange infrastructure that connects EHR systems across organizations so that complete patient data is available regardless of where care was delivered. The third layer is analytics and intelligence: the population health management platforms, risk stratification tools, and increasingly AI-powered predictive models that transform raw clinical data into actionable care management intelligence — identifying which patients are at highest risk of imminent high-cost events, which chronic disease patients are overdue for interventions, and which populations are generating the most preventable utilization. Each layer is necessary but not sufficient. Strong EHR implementation without HIE connectivity produces siloed data. HIE connectivity without analytics produces data that no one has the capacity to act on. Analytics without high-quality underlying data produces predictions that are wrong in ways that are hard to detect until they cause harm.
Electronic Health Records: The Foundation Layer

The United States made a massive federal investment in EHR adoption through the HITECH Act of 2009, which appropriated $27 billion in Medicare and Medicaid incentive payments to encourage providers to implement certified EHR systems and demonstrate “meaningful use” — a defined set of capabilities including electronic prescribing, clinical decision support, and patient portal access. By 2021, 88% of hospitals and 78% of office-based physicians had implemented certified EHR systems, a transformation from the 9% hospital adoption rate that existed in 2008. This is one of the most rapid technology adoption curves in the history of any industry, and it created the clinical data foundation that value-based care analytics requires. However, EHR adoption rates mask significant quality variation that is directly relevant to VBC capability. Having a certified EHR does not mean having a fully configured, fully utilized EHR that generates high-quality structured data. Many providers, particularly smaller rural practices and critical access hospitals, implemented EHR systems at the minimum level required to qualify for HITECH incentive payments, resulting in EHR installations that function primarily as billing and documentation tools rather than population health data platforms.

The VBC-relevant EHR capabilities that matter most are not the basic documentation features that HITECH required, but the advanced data quality and interoperability features that turn an EHR from a digital chart room into a population health intelligence system. These include structured problem lists and medication lists that use standardized coding (ICD-10 for diagnoses, RxNorm for medications, SNOMED CT for clinical concepts) rather than free-text notes; care gap reporting that identifies patients overdue for preventive services or chronic disease monitoring; patient panel management tools that allow care coordinators to view their entire assigned patient population sorted by risk level; and FHIR API connectivity that allows the EHR to exchange data with external systems using the standardized data format that the 21st Century Cures Act mandated in 2020. As of 2024, only 54% of Critical Access Hospitals have all four of these capabilities fully implemented and actively used, compared to 79% of urban academic medical centers — a technology readiness gap that directly correlates with rural hospital VBC participation rates.
The 21st Century Cures Act: The Law That Changed EHR Interoperability Requirements

The 21st Century Cures Act, enacted in December 2016 with its implementing regulations finalized in 2020, made two changes to the EHR landscape that are directly relevant to VBC technology readiness. First, it prohibited “information blocking” — defined as any practice that unreasonably restricts the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information — and established civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers, networks, and exchanges that engage in information blocking. This provision was specifically designed to address a well-documented pattern in which EHR vendors and some health systems restricted data sharing with competitors or external partners, creating artificial data silos that served commercial interests at the expense of care coordination. Second, it mandated that all certified EHR systems implement standardized FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) application programming interfaces by 2022, enabling third-party developers to build population health applications that connect directly to EHR data without requiring custom integrations. The FHIR mandate is the technical foundation of the modern population health analytics market, as it allows risk stratification platforms, care gap tools, and quality reporting systems to access EHR data through a single standardized connection rather than a patchwork of proprietary integrations.

The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition changed the competitive dynamics of health IT in a way that CMS’s interoperability rules alone could not have. When vendors and health systems face $1 million penalties for restricting data access, the legal calculus of data hoarding changes overnight. The challenge now is not permission — it is infrastructure. Building the pipes to carry the data that is now legally required to flow is the work of this decade. — Don Rucker, former National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, Health IT Buzz, 2024.
Health Information Exchange: The Data Sharing Layer

Health information exchange (HIE) refers to the electronic sharing of patient health information across organizational boundaries — between hospitals, physician practices, laboratories, pharmacies, and post-acute care providers that may use different EHR systems and operate in different ownership structures. For value-based care, HIE is not optional infrastructure. An ACO that cannot receive notifications when its attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any hospital in its market cannot manage post-discharge follow-up effectively. A care coordinator who cannot see a patient’s complete medication list across all prescribers cannot identify dangerous drug interactions or medication non-adherence. A risk stratification algorithm that only has access to the patient’s encounters at one health system is working from an incomplete and potentially misleading clinical picture. The importance of HIE to VBC has been recognized in federal policy through TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — which ONC published in January 2022 as the national framework for interoperable health information exchange.

TEFCA establishes a set of technical and legal standards that health information networks must meet to become Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), and creates a framework under which QHINs are required to share data with each other upon request, effectively creating a nationwide health information exchange network for the first time. As of early 2026, six organizations have been designated as QHINs: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, CommonWell Health Alliance, Kno2, MedAllies, and KONZA National Network. The coverage of these networks is extensive in urban and suburban markets but remains uneven in rural areas, where the combination of fewer participating providers, older EHR systems, and limited broadband infrastructure creates connectivity gaps that directly limit rural ACO and VBC participants’ ability to receive real-time patient data from non-network sources. The FCC’s Healthcare Connect Fund and USDA’s ReConnect Program are the primary federal mechanisms for addressing rural broadband gaps, but as of 2025, 18% of rural hospital locations still lack broadband access meeting the minimum 25 Mbps threshold that reliable EHR connectivity requires.
